title: Ideal Bose-Einstein condensation in the canonical ensemble: exact asymptotic estimates from large deviations
authors: Giacomo Gradenigo, Dario Lucente, Luca Salasnich
abstract: In this work we present a large-deviations approach to the calculation of the canonical partition function for free bosons. Three-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensation is studied in the fixed-density ensemble as a function of the dimensionless density $\varrho = ρλ_T^3$, with $ρ=N/L^3$ the standard particle density, $λ_T$ the thermal wavelength, $L$ the linear size of the box and $N$ the total number of particles. A large-deviations approach in terms of the dimensionless parameter $\ell=L/λ_T$ allows us to provide exact asymptotic estimates of the canonical partition function both above and below the critical density $\varrho_c$ for Bose-Einstein condensation. We show how this approach allows to explicitly account for finite-size effects and how it fully captures the first-order aspects of the transition, allowing us to explicitate its driving mechanism in terms of the competing probabilities of normal and condensed phases. The proposed large-deviations approach allows then to obtain in all regimes explicit and simple analytical expressions, at the leading order in the large parameter $\ell$, for both the average fraction of particles in the ground state, the condensate fraction $\langle n_0(\varrho) \rangle = \langle N_0(\varrho) \rangle/N$, and for its fluctuations, $σ_0(\varrho) = \sqrt{\langle N_0^2(\varrho)\rangle - \langle N_0(\varrho)\rangle^2}/N$, retrieving for instance the anomalous scaling $σ_0(\varrho)\sim 1/V^{1/3}$ in the condensed regime, $\varrho > \varrho_c$. Our large-deviations asymptotic estimate, by analytically clarifying the mixed-order nature of Bose-Einstein condensation, allows then to reveal the similarity between this transition and other mixed-order transitions, as for instance the localization transition in the Discrete Non-Linear Schrödinger Equation.
summary: This work develops a large-deviations approach to calculate the canonical partition function for free bosons undergoing BEC. By analyzing the fixed-density ensemble, the authors obtain exact asymptotic estimates for key observables like the condensate fraction and its fluctuations in all regimes relative to the critical density. This method clarifies the mixed-order nature of the BEC transition and provides analytical tools applicable to other complex phase transitions.
main_problem: To derive exact asymptotic estimates for the canonical partition function of free bosons undergoing Bose-Einstein Condensation (BEC) using a large-deviations approach.
main_result: The large-deviations method provides explicit, simple analytical expressions for the condensate fraction and its fluctuations in both the normal and condensed regimes, revealing the mixed-order nature of the transition.
method: The core method is applying large-deviations theory to the fixed-density (canonical) ensemble, involving complex contour integration and asymptotic analysis in the limit of large system size ($\ell 	o \infty$).
model_or_system: The system is an ideal, non-interacting gas of bosons confined in a three-dimensional box. The analysis focuses on the fixed-density ensemble, contrasting it with standard grand-canonical approaches.
key_observables: Average condensate fraction $\langle n_0(\varrho) angle$, condensate fraction fluctuations $\sigma_0(\varrho)$, and the canonical partition function $Z(N)$.
important_parameters: Dimensionless density $\varrho = ho \lambda_T^3$, the large-deviations parameter $\ell = L/\lambda_T$, and the critical density $\varrho_c$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to free bosons, and the method relies on asymptotic expansions in the large parameter $\ell$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting the canonical and grand-canonical ensembles. It then develops the large-deviations framework, providing explicit calculations for the partition function and observables in both regimes ($\varrho < \varrho_c$ and $\varrho > \varrho_c$) using complex analysis techniques.
why_interesting: The rigorous treatment of the canonical ensemble, especially resolving the first-order nature of the transition and providing fluctuation scaling laws, offers a powerful theoretical tool applicable to other mixed-order phase transitions.
